question.text: Mr. Rajesh Menon, CIO of Lotus Alternative Partners, is computing the hurdle rate for a new Category II AIF focused on private credit. He decomposes the required rate of return into its three canonical components. Which of the following correctly identifies all THREE components per NISM Chapter 1?

answer.text: Real risk-free rate + expected inflation + risk premium
Nominal risk-free rate + beta + liquidity discount
Real risk-free rate + equity risk premium + alpha
Government bond yield + credit spread + management fee

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Chapter 1.4, Required Rate of Return = Real risk-free rate + Inflation adjustment + Risk premium adjustment. The real risk-free rate compensates for pure postponement of consumption, the inflation component preserves purchasing power, and the risk premium compensates for uncertainty around future cashflows. The nominal risk-free rate already bundles the first two components. The Trap: Option B double-counts — nominal rate already includes inflation, and 'beta' is a CAPM sensitivity, not a component of the required return formula. Option C confuses alpha (realised excess return) with the ex-ante risk premium. Option D is the credit trader's heuristic but mixes a fee (management fee) into the return demanded — fees come out of, not into, the required return. Cross-Exam Context: XXI-B (Portfolio Manager) tests this with CAPM overlay; X-A and X-B (IA) test the Fisher form; XV (RA) tests the decomposition for cost-of-equity estimation. Manager's Pro-Tip: When pitching to LPs, show the hurdle rate decomposition on a bridge slide (e.g., 'we target 18% net IRR = 7% real rate + 5% inflation + 6% illiquidity/private-market premium'). LPs push back on round-number hurdles; a decomposed number survives diligence.
